archetype.name: Point Guard (short-area distributor)
archetype.definition: A quick-game point guard in Sean Payton's offense who wins by getting the ball out short and on schedule, spreading it across five regular targets and almost never taking a sack, rather than by pushing the ball downfield.

report.headline: Ultra-safe short game carries a 7-2 team; third downs and middle throws hold him back
report.take:
Bo Nix in year three is a low-risk distributor. His intended air yards sit at 6.37, his average throw lands 2.48 yards short of the sticks, and 219 of his 287 charted attempts travel under 10 air yards. The payoff is protection of the football and of himself: a 3.7% sack rate (3rd of 54), a 17.5% pressure-to-sack rate (5th of 42) and a 1.4% interception rate (16th). The cost is reach. His 6.03 yards per attempt ranks 40th, and his 0.019 EPA per dropback is only 26th, essentially average for a qualifier. The 7-2 record leans on a defense that ranks 2nd in hit rate as much as on him.

The EPA ledger shows where the offense lives and where it leaks. Throws of 0-9 air yards are the engine, with +23.3 EPA and a +4.5 CPOE. The 78 throws behind the line, the screens and swing passes Payton uses as a run substitute, give back -13.6. The 10-19 yard window is the real flaw: 41.5% completions, a -10.7 CPOE and three of his four interceptions. Throws over the middle are almost absent, and he hits only 39.3% of them. Third down concentrates every one of those problems. He faces an average of 7.7 yards to go, throws short of the sticks by habit, and converts 26.7% at -0.302 EPA a play, a -26 EPA hole that by itself erases most of his season's value.

The arc across his career matters too. Completion rate has slid from 66.3% to 63.4% to 60.6%, yards per attempt from 6.66 to 6.42 to 6.03, and rushing from 20.9 yards a game last year to 12.9. Designed runs are getting stuffed 30% of the time at 1.65 yards a carry. He has always been a below-average CPOE passer who avoids sacks, so none of that is new. What is new is that the legs aren't making up the difference. The scrambles still work, at 0.25 EPA each, but there are only eight of them.

The last three games are why this card isn't gloomier. From Week 7 to Week 9 he posted 0.16 EPA per dropback and 7.45 ANY/A, with CPOE flipped positive. That came against Arizona (31st-ranked defense), Kansas City (6th) and Carolina (19th), so it isn't purely a soft-schedule mirage. The 27-attempt deep sample (0.275 EPA) and Pat Bryant's 0.834 EPA per target on 18 looks are giving the offense some explosiveness. Both are small samples, so they are hints rather than proof. Expect a passer in the 0.05-0.10 EPA range from here, steadier than the early-October version and still capped by the middle of the field.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance that holds up
strengths.body: He takes sacks on 3.7% of dropbacks against a league average of 7.9%, and turns only 17.5% of pressures into sacks. Some of that is a line that ranks 2nd in offensive hit rate. Most of it is his own quick, short decision-making. His pressure-to-sack rate ranked 7th last season too, so this is a career trait, not a hot streak, and it keeps drives alive that a riskier passer would kill.

strengths.title: Accurate, productive short game
strengths.body: Throws of 0-9 air yards are the core of the offense: 141 attempts, 68.8% completions, a +4.5 CPOE and +23.3 EPA. Seven of his 11 touchdowns come from this range, which is how a modest-yardage passer still finishes drives, as his nine red-zone TDs show. This is repeatable because it is how the offense is built, not a byproduct of a few big plays.

strengths.title: Composure in tight fourth quarters
strengths.body: In close fourth quarters he has produced 0.187 EPA per play, well above his overall rate, and the 7-2 record includes several one-score wins. The 48-play sample is small, but it fits a passer whose game is built on not giving the ball away. It is a useful tiebreaker, not a pillar of the projection.

concerns.title: Third downs are a sinkhole
concerns.body: He converts 26.7% of third downs at -0.302 EPA a play, with an average of 7.7 yards to go. This is the price of the scheme. Early downs lean on screens and short throws that leave long third downs, and his habit of throwing short of the sticks doesn't fit those situations. Until the intermediate game works, this persists. It is the main reason a 7-2 offense ranks 27th in success rate.

concerns.title: The 10-19 yard window
concerns.body: Intermediate throws produce 41.5% completions, a -10.7 CPOE and three of his four interceptions, and he rarely attacks the middle of the field. This is a real accuracy and anticipation gap, not a role artifact. His badThrowPct has been in the bottom half for three straight seasons. It caps his ceiling and explains why Courtland Sutton, a high-volume target, sits at -5.3 EPA.

concerns.title: Efficiency and legs both trending down
concerns.body: Yards per attempt has fallen for three straight seasons, and his rushing is off 8.1 yards a game from last year. Designed runs average 1.65 yards with a 30% stuff rate, so the rushing floor that propped up his early-career value has thinned. The scrambles still pay (0.25 EPA each). The question is whether Payton keeps calling the designed runs that aren't working.

trend.note: His low point came in Weeks 5-6, when he posted negative passing EPA against the Chargers and Seattle. He then followed with +2.9, +6.6 and +6.6 in Weeks 7-9, and his last-three EPA per dropback runs 0.141 above his season rate. The KC and Carolina games make it more than an Arizona-driven blip.

nextGame.headline: Bye-rested Nix gets the league's worst short-pass defense
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas is close to an ideal opponent for this profile. The Raiders rank 32nd in success rate allowed and 32nd against short passes, at 0.243 EPA, exactly the range where Nix does his damage. They also allow quarterbacks 2.5 touchdowns a game (31st) and 19.9 PPR (29th). Two catches: they get home, ranking 7th in hit rate, and a 10-point spread raises the chance Denver plays with a two-score lead. In that state Nix has been poor (-0.317 EPA on 27 plays) and the offense tends to lean on the run, which could clip his volume.

Availability is the swing on his side. Jaylen Waddle, his most-targeted receiver and one of only two positive-EPA wideouts, left Week 9 with a concussion and is listed questionable. The bye gives him 14 days to clear protocol. If he sits, more volume goes to Pat Bryant's small but explosive sample and to Sutton, whose results have been negative. On the Raiders' side, DT Thomas Booker IV was out last week and edge Kwity Paye is questionable with a neck injury, which could thin the rush that is LV's one defensive strength. Kickoff weather is days away but currently looks benign.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. a soft underneath zone
keyMatchups.body: LV is last in short-pass EPA allowed, and Nix's 0-9 yard throws are his best area by a wide margin. Expect quick completions to stay on schedule, which should also ease his third-down problem by shortening the distance.

keyMatchups.title: Secondary options vs. weak coverage
keyMatchups.body: LV has let WR2s run 4.8 PPR over their averages (32nd) and lead backs 4.2 over (31st), while holding WR1s under. That tilts targets toward the second receiver and RJ Harvey, whose 0.169 EPA per target is among Nix's better connections. It matters more if Waddle is out and the pecking order shifts.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script risk
keyMatchups.body: A 10-point spread and a 40.5 total point to Denver leading comfortably. When ahead by 9+, Nix's efficiency has collapsed and the volume usually goes away. Efficient early drives could still leave him with a modest final line.

nextGame.watch: Whether Waddle clears the concussion protocol. Without him, the question becomes whether Nix finally attacks LV's intermediate zones or keeps everything behind the sticks.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts of his game that should hold are the low sack rate, the low interception rate and the short-area efficiency. They have shown up across three seasons and are built into Payton's design. Volume should stay steady in the low 30s attempts with a pass-leaning offense (6th in pass rate over expected), so expect something like 195-245 passing yards and 1.2-1.8 touchdowns a game. That is better than his full-season rate, because the last three weeks look more like his true level than the October trough did. It is not the 2024-25 ceiling, though, because the intermediate accuracy hasn't improved.

What will regress is the edge. Bryant's per-target efficiency and the 0.275 deep EPA rest on tiny samples, and the red-zone touchdown rate on 45 attempts is hard to bank on. The rushing floor is thinner than in past years. A 10-25 rush-yard range assumes the designed-run game stays stuffed and scrambles remain rare. Fantasy value lands at 14-20 PPR a game: a steady mid-tier QB, not a weekly difference-maker.
swingFactors: Game scripts: big leads suppress his volume

confidence.note: Nine starts, three-year consistent profile; recent surge partly vs. weak defense, Waddle uncertain.
